title: Prompt Caching: How It Works, What It Costs, and How to Keep the Cache Hitting
summary: How prompt caching works on Anthropic, OpenAI, and Gemini: KV cache basics, 2026 pricing, break-even math, and layout rules that keep agents hitting the cache.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


Question Answer (October 2026) Source


What does a cache read cost? **0.025x** to **0.1x** of base input on Anthropic, **0.05x** to **0.1x** on OpenAI's GPT-5.6+[Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) ,[OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)


What does a cache write cost? **1.25x** (5-minute) or **2x** (1-hour) on Anthropic, **1.25x** on GPT-5.6+, nothing extra on Gemini implicit caching Provider docs


When does a write pay for itself? After **one** reuse at the 1.25x tier, **two** at the 1-hour tier Break-even table in this post


How much does it save on real agents? **49-80%** lower token cost across Anthropic, OpenAI, and Gemini on LangChain's agent evals[LangChain, June 2026](https://www.langchain.com/blog/deep-agents-prompt-caching)


What hit rates do teams get? **77%** on Anthropic direct, **24%** for the same Claude models on Vertex, across a gateway's April 2026 traffic[Requesty](https://www.requesty.ai/data/cache-hit-rate-by-provider-april-2026)


What breaks it? Any byte change before the breakpoint: timestamps, tool changes, model or effort switches, unstable JSON, idle gaps Provider docs


Caching is a prefix match, so put everything that never changes at the start of the request and everything that changes at the end. Then measure your hit rate per request and alert when it drops.


---


In April 2026, the AI gateway Requesty measured prompt cache hit rates across its traffic. Requests to Claude through Anthropic's own API[read 77% of their input tokens from cache](https://www.requesty.ai/data/cache-hit-rate-by-provider-april-2026) . Requests to Claude through Google's Vertex read 24%. The models were the same, and the gateway called the gap a configuration problem.


Anthropic's Claude Code team alerts on cache hit rate and treats a drop as an incident, and OpenAI shipped a dashboard and a miss-diagnostics field for it in September 2026.


> It is often said in engineering that 'Cache Rules Everything Around Me', and the same rule holds for agents.


—[Thariq Shihipar](https://x.com/trq212) , member of the Claude Code team at Anthropic


For the broader cost picture,[LLM token optimization](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/llm-token-optimization) covers caching alongside eight other techniques.


## What is prompt caching?


Prompt caching is an LLM API feature that stores the processed state of the beginning of a prompt so later requests starting with the same tokens skip reprocessing them. Cached tokens cost between 0.025x and 0.1x the normal input price on current Anthropic and OpenAI models, and responses start sooner because the model has less input to process.


Model APIs are stateless. Every turn of a chat or agent loop resends the system prompt, the tool definitions, and the whole conversation so far, and the model processes all of it again. In[an April 2026 study of eight frontier models on SWE-bench Verified](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22750) , Longju Bai and colleagues found agentic coding tasks consumed 1,000x more tokens than code chat, with input tokens driving most of the cost.


Prompt caching never changes the output. Anthropic's docs state the response is[identical to what you would get without caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) .


## How does prompt caching work?


An LLM handles a request in two phases:


- **Prefill** reads the whole input in parallel and, at every layer, computes a key vector and a value vector for every token.
- **Decode** then generates the output one token at a time, and each new token attends to the keys and values of everything before it.


Those stored key and value vectors are the KV cache.


Within a single request, the KV cache saves the model from recomputing earlier tokens at each decode step. Prompt caching extends that across requests. The provider keeps the KV tensors for a prompt prefix after the request ends, and reuses them when the next request starts the same way. OpenAI's guide states that[the cache stores KV tensors](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) rather than the tokens.


Reuse only works for a prefix because attention in these models is causal. The key and value vectors for token 500 depend on tokens 1 through 499 and nothing after. Change token 12, and the vectors for every token from 12 onward come out different, so the saved state is useless from that point. Change only the last message, and everything before it is still valid.


Providers implement the lookup with hashes. On Anthropic, marking a block with` cache_control` writes one cache entry keyed by[a cumulative hash of everything up to that block](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) . On the next request, the API computes the hash at your breakpoint, and if there is no match it walks backward up to 20 blocks looking for an entry an earlier request wrote.


A three-turn conversation with Anthropic's automatic caching, which moves the breakpoint to the last block on every request, looks like this:


```text
Request 1:  [system + tools][user 1]                                 -> write all
Request 2:  [system + tools][user 1][asst 1][user 2]                 -> read through user 1, write asst 1 + user 2
Request 3:  [system + tools][user 1][asst 1][user 2][asst 2][user 3] -> read through user 2, write asst 2 + user 3
```


Self-hosted inference engines do the same thing in memory. vLLM's automatic prefix caching hashes fixed-size blocks of KV cache so identical prefixes share blocks, and SGLang's RadixAttention keeps cached prefixes in a radix tree so requests that share a beginning share the work.


## What's the difference between prompt caching, semantic caching, and KV caching?


KV caching Prompt caching Semantic caching


What is stored Key and value vectors for tokens in the current request KV state for a prompt prefix, kept between requests Complete responses, keyed by an embedding of the query


Where it lives GPU memory during one request Provider's serving infrastructure Your application (Redis, a vector store)


Match rule Automatic within a request Byte-identical prefix Similarity above a threshold


Does the model run? Yes Yes, on the uncached suffix No, on a hit


Can it change the answer? No No Yes, it can return a stale or wrong answer


Best for Every request Agents, chat, long shared documents FAQ-style traffic with near-duplicate questions


Semantic caching helps when many users ask nearly the same question. Agents rarely do, because each request carries its own history, so prefix caching does almost all the work there.


## Prompt caching on Anthropic, OpenAI, and Gemini


The three major APIs all cache by prefix, but they differ in who places the breakpoints, how long entries live, and whether a write costs extra:


Anthropic (Claude API) OpenAI (GPT-5.6 and later) Google Gemini API


How to turn it on Top-level` cache_control` (automatic) or up to 4 block-level breakpoints On by default; implicit, explicit, or both On by default (implicit) for Gemini 2.5 and newer


Minimum prefix 512 tokens on current models; 1,024 to 4,096 on older ones 1,024 visible input tokens 4,096 on Gemini 4 Argon and 3.x; 2,048 on 2.5


Cache lifetime 5 minutes, refreshed on each hit; 1-hour option At least 30 minutes after last write or reuse Not published


Write price 1.25x (5-minute), 2x (1-hour) 1.25x No premium


Read price 0.1x; 0.05x on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5; 0.025x on Fable 5.1 0.1x; 0.05x on GPT-6.1 Sol Discounted, with no guaranteed hit


Usage field` cache_read_input_tokens` ,` cache_creation_input_tokens`` cached_tokens` ,` cache_write_tokens`` total_cached_tokens`


Miss diagnostics` diagnostics.cache_miss_reason`` prompt_cache_diagnostics` and a dashboard Not documented


Pre-warming` max_tokens: 0` request Supported Not documented


*Sources:[Anthropic prompt caching docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) ,[OpenAI prompt caching guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) , and[Gemini context caching docs](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching) , all read October 18, 2026.*


### Anthropic prompt caching


Claude prompt caching is opt-in. The quickest setup is[automatic caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/overview) , launched February 19, 2026: add one top-level` cache_control` field, and the API caches everything up to the last cacheable block and moves that point forward as the conversation grows.


```text
import   anthropic


client   =   anthropic  .  Anthropic  ()


response   =   client  .  messages  .  create  (
model  =  "claude-sonnet-5-5"  ,
max_tokens  =  1024  ,
cache_control  =  {  "type"  :   "ephemeral"  },    # automatic caching
system  =  "You are a support agent for Acme. <policies>...</policies>"  ,
messages  =  [{  "role"  :   "user"  ,   "content"  :   "Can I get a refund after 30 days?"  }],
)


u   =   response  .  usage
print  (u.cache_creation_input_tokens, u.cache_read_input_tokens, u.input_tokens)
```


Explicit breakpoints go on individual blocks when sections change at different rates, for example tools that never change, a document that changes daily, and a conversation that changes every turn. You get four breakpoints per request, and the automatic one uses a slot. Cache prefixes build in a fixed order,` tools` , then` system` , then` messages` , and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it.


Three Anthropic details trip people up:


- **Lifetime counts from the start of the request.** The docs give the example of a response that takes 4 minutes to stream: the follow-up must start within about 1 minute of it finishing to hit the 5-minute cache.
- **Parallel requests don't share a cache until the first response starts.** If you fan out ten requests with the same prefix at once, all ten write. Send one, wait for it to start responding, then send the rest.
- **Some settings live inside the cached prefix.** Changing tool definitions invalidates everything. Toggling web search, citations, or fast mode invalidates the system and message caches. Changing` tool_choice` , images, the thinking configuration, or the effort setting invalidates message blocks.


Mid-conversation system messages let you send` role: "system"` updates inside` messages` without rewriting the cached prefix, and the[September 2026 release notes](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/overview) list betas that do the same for per-message effort changes and for defining new tools inside a message.


### OpenAI prompt caching


OpenAI prompt caching is on by default. On GPT-5.6 and later,[implicit mode places a breakpoint](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) at the end of the latest eligible message, and explicit mode lets you mark breakpoints yourself, with up to four cache writes per request. Content after your last explicit breakpoint is billed at the plain input rate with no write charge, which is useful for content you don't expect to reuse.


```text
from   openai   import   OpenAI


client   =   OpenAI  ()


response   =   client  .  responses  .  create  (
model  =  "gpt-6.1-sol"  ,
prompt_cache_options  =  {  "mode"  :   "explicit"  },
input  =  [
{
"role"  :   "developer"  ,
"content"  : [{
"type"  :   "input_text"  ,
"text"  : SYSTEM_PROMPT_AND_REFERENCE_DOCS,
"prompt_cache_breakpoint"  : {  "mode"  :   "explicit"  },
}],
},
{  "role"  :   "user"  ,   "content"  :   "Summarize the refund policy."  },
],
)


print  (response.usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens)
```


Cached state[lives on individual machines](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) , and traffic above 15 requests per minute can overflow to machines that don't hold the entry. On models before GPT-5.6, a stable` prompt_cache_key` such as a user or session ID helps route related requests to the same cache; on GPT-5.6 and later, OpenAI routes automatically and the key is only for separating cache accounting.


OpenAI's[September 22, 2026 announcement](https://openai.com/index/better-prompt-caching-for-gpt-6/) also added a way to change reasoning effort mid-conversation without breaking the cache: append a` configuration_update` input item and leave the request-level` reasoning.effort` unchanged. To restrict tools for one turn, use` allowed_tools` or` tool_choice: "none"` instead of removing definitions.


### Gemini prompt caching


Gemini's API caches implicitly for[Gemini 2.5 and newer models](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching) , in both stateful and stateless conversations, with no configuration. Google's advice is to put large, common content at the start of the prompt and send requests with similar prefixes close together. Cache hits appear in` usage.total_cached_tokens` .


Gemini's higher minimum (4,096 tokens on current models) means short prompts never cache, and implicit caching makes no hit guarantee.


xAI also discounts cached input. Its[September 2026 release notes](https://docs.x.ai/developers/release-notes) list Grok 4.7 at $2 input and $0.50 cached input per million tokens, so a cached token costs a quarter of a fresh one.


## How much does prompt caching cost?


These are list prices per million tokens from[Anthropic's caching docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) and[OpenAI's pricing page](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing) on October 18, 2026:


Model Input 5-min write 1-hour write Cache read Read as share of input


Claude Fable 5.1 $10.00 $12.50 $20.00 $0.25 2.5%


Claude Opus 5.5 $4.00 $5.00 $8.00 $0.20 5%


Claude Sonnet 5.5 $2.00 $2.50 $4.00 $0.10 5%


Claude Haiku 5.5 (up to 100k tokens) $0.10 $0.125 $0.20 $0.01 10%


GPT-6 Astra $10.00 $12.50 n/a $1.00 10%


GPT-6.1 Sol $2.00 $2.50 n/a $0.10 5%


GPT-6 Luna $0.10 $0.125 n/a $0.01 10%


*Standard short-context rates. OpenAI's write column is its single cache-write rate.*


Read prices have been falling. Anthropic[cut cache reads on Fable 5.1](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/overview) to 0.025x at launch on September 1, 2026, and on October 7 halved Sonnet 5.5 reads from $0.20 to $0.10. Write prices stayed the same, so writes now carry a larger share of the bill. In our[Fable 5.1 vs Fable 5 runs](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/is-fable-5-1-cheaper-than-fable-5) , the newer model only came out cheaper on cache-heavy work for this reason.


### When does a cache write pay for itself?


Think of a cached prefix in multiples of its normal input cost. With a write premium of` w` and a read price of` r` , caching the prefix and reusing it` n` times costs` w + n·r` , against` 1 + n` without caching.


Pricing Cost for 1 use + 1 reuse Without caching Pays off after


Anthropic 5-min write, 0.05x read (Sonnet 5.5) 1.30 2.00 1 reuse


Anthropic 1-hour write, 0.05x read 2.05 2.00 2 reuses


OpenAI GPT-5.6+, 0.1x read 1.35 2.00 1 reuse


Earlier OpenAI models, Gemini implicit (no write premium) Cheaper from the first hit Immediately


The 1-hour tier only pays when gaps between requests are longer than 5 minutes, and only if the prefix is reused at least twice. If requests come more often than every 5 minutes, the 5-minute cache refreshes itself for free on each hit.


A 5-minute cache on requests that arrive more than 5 minutes apart is a loss. Each request misses, writes again at 1.25x, and you pay 25% more than you would with no caching at all.


BenchLM ran this as a live test on[September 14, 2026](https://benchlm.ai/blog/posts/prompt-caching) , sending 87 calls each to Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 Terra through OpenRouter with a shared long system prompt. The first Sonnet call cost 24.7% more than the uncached equivalent, the second cost 89.1% less, and input spend across all 87 calls fell 87.8%, with 97.9% of input tokens read from cache.


## How much does prompt caching save on a real agent?


Take a support agent on Claude Sonnet 5.5 with a 20,000-token static prefix (system prompt plus tool definitions). Each of its 10 turns adds 3,000 tokens of user message and tool results and writes a 500-token reply. Over the session, it processes 387,500 input tokens.


Configuration Cost per session vs no caching


No caching $0.825


Automatic caching, prefix stable $0.220 **73% lower**


Caching on, timestamp in the system prompt $1.019 **23% higher**


*Anthropic list prices, October 18, 2026. Output is $0.05 of each total. With a stable prefix, 85.9% of input tokens are read from cache.*


In the third row, a timestamp at the top of the system prompt changes the hash on every request, so every turn writes the full context at 1.25x and nothing is ever read. The API returns no error when this happens.


On LangChain's[Deep Agents eval suite in June 2026](https://www.langchain.com/blog/deep-agents-prompt-caching) , prompt caching cut token cost by 77% on Claude Haiku 4.5 using explicit breakpoints, 80% on GPT-5.4 mini with OpenAI's automatic caching, and 49% on Gemini 3.5 Flash with implicit caching. The longer the trajectory, the more the cached prefix gets reused.


## 10 rules for a high cache hit rate in agents


### 1. Order the prompt from static to dynamic


Claude Code orders its requests as static system prompt and tools (shared across all users), then project context such as CLAUDE.md (shared within a project), then session context, then messages. The[Claude Code caching docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching) describe the same three layers: a change to the conversation leaves the system prompt and project context cached, and a change to the system prompt invalidates everything.


For any app, the order is: tools, instructions, few-shot examples and reference documents, per-user context, conversation history, the new message.


### 2. Move changing values out of the prefix


Timestamps, request IDs, user names, and feature flags at the top of a prompt break the cache on every request. Pass them in the latest user message or tool result instead. Claude Code adds a` <system-reminder>` tag to the next message with updates like the current date rather than editing the system prompt.


On Anthropic, also place your breakpoint on the last block that stays identical. If you put` cache_control` on a block that includes the changing value, the docs explain, the API writes a new entry at that block on every request and the backward lookup never finds a prior write at an earlier position.


### 3. Serialize deterministically


The cache matches bytes, so two JSON objects with the same content in a different key order are different prefixes. Anthropic's troubleshooting list calls out[languages like Swift and Go](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) that randomize key order during JSON conversion. Sort keys when you build tool schemas and tool results, and don't regenerate tool descriptions from templates that can change between requests.


### 4. Keep the tool list fixed for the session


Tool definitions sit at the very start of the prefix, so adding, removing, or reordering one invalidates the entire cache. Claude Code keeps every tool loaded and models state changes as tool calls instead. Turning on plan mode calls an` EnterPlanMode` tool and adds a system message, and the tool definitions stay the same.


For large tool catalogs, defer instead of removing. Anthropic's tool search sends lightweight stubs and loads a full schema only when the model asks for it, so the stubs stay the same on every request. On OpenAI, keep the full` tools` list and narrow it per turn with` allowed_tools` .


Adding web access mid-session has the same cost. Unless your harness defers tool loading, connecting an MCP server adds tool definitions and invalidates the cache, while a CLI the agent runs through its existing shell tool, such as the Firecrawl CLI, adds none. We compared the two approaches in[MCP vs CLI for AI agents](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/mcp-vs-cli) .


### 5. Do the math before switching models


Each model has its own cache. Thariq's example was that 100,000 tokens into an Opus conversation, asking Haiku an easy question costs more than letting Opus answer, because Haiku has to rebuild the cache.


At Anthropic's October 2026 rates, the answer depends on how long the context is, because Haiku 5.5 charges more for prompts over 100,000 tokens:


Context Opus 5.5 reading it from cache Haiku 5.5 processing it fresh Cheaper


150,000 tokens $0.030 ($0.20 per million) $0.075 ($0.50 per million, long-context rate) Opus


80,000 tokens $0.016 ($0.20 per million) $0.008 ($0.10 per million) Haiku


Even when Haiku is cheaper, it has to prefill the whole context before it answers, so the first token arrives later. When you do need a cheaper model, hand it a short summary through a subagent rather than switching the main session.


### 6. Pick effort and thinking settings once


Effort and thinking settings are rendered into the prompt on many models, so changing them mid-session can invalidate the cache. The Claude Code docs note that on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Fable 5.1, with an API key or a Claude subscription, the cache stays intact by default when effort changes. On other models, or through your own API calls, use the provider's mid-conversation mechanism: OpenAI's` configuration_update` item or Anthropic's per-message effort beta.


### 7. Fork side tasks from the parent's prefix


Compaction, summarization, and background checks are separate API calls. Built the simple way, with a different system prompt and no tools, they miss the cache and pay full price for the whole conversation. Claude Code's compaction reuses the parent's exact system prompt, tools, and history, then appends the summary instruction as a new user message, so only that instruction is new.


### 8. Match the TTL to the gaps in your traffic


Measure the time between turns in your own logs. If most gaps are under 5 minutes, use the 5-minute cache. If users or agents routinely pause for 5 to 60 minutes, the 1-hour tier saves a full rewrite each time.


On Hacker News in April, Boris Cherny of the Claude Code team[explained](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47880089) that returning to a session after more than an hour idle is a full cache miss on every message, and that a 900,000-token context would write more than 900,000 tokens to cache in one turn. A reply in the[942-point thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47878905)[objected to calling that a corner case](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47887640) , since leaving sessions idle over lunch is normal. If your product lets users resume old sessions, warn them or compact before resuming.


### 9. Pre-warm the cache before users arrive


The first request after a deploy or a cache expiry pays the full write and the slowest time to first token. Anthropic lets you send a request with` max_tokens: 0` , which writes the cache at your breakpoints and returns immediately with no output. OpenAI added prewarming in September as well. Fire one at startup or on a schedule shorter than the TTL, with the same thinking and effort settings your real requests use.


### 10. Check that your gateway passes cache markers through


The Claude Code docs describe three gateway behaviors:[forwarding markers unchanged, rejecting them with a 400, or silently removing them](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching) , in which case the entire conversation bills as uncached input on every turn. Converting block-form system content to a plain string drops the marker the same way. A stripped marker could explain part of the Vertex gap in Requesty's data.


Model routers have the same problem. In a[June 2026 Show HN for a model router](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48688700) , commenters pointed out that every switch is a fresh cache miss, and one[described handing plans to a single model](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48697586) that held 99.9% cache hits over a long session.


## Where should web content go in a cached prompt?


Append fetched pages as tool results at the end of the conversation and leave them there. Re-fetching a page and splicing the new copy into an earlier position changes the prefix from that point on, and live pages change between loads.


To measure how often, we scraped eight pages with Firecrawl twice, 90 seconds apart, with its page cache turned off (` maxAge: 0` ), then twice more with the cache on:


Page Words Two live scrapes Two cached scrapes


Hacker News front page 1,016 Different (point counts) Identical


BBC News 1,763 Different ("minutes ago" labels) Identical


Yahoo Finance AAPL quote 770 Different (AI news summary) Identical


GitHub Trending 1,830 Different Identical


The Verge home page 6,087 Different Identical


Wikipedia, "Large language model" 17,477 Different (page layout) Identical


Python` json` docs 4,476 Identical Identical


Stripe pricing 4,070 Identical Identical


*Firecrawl scrape with` onlyMainContent` , October 18, 2026. Cached runs used` maxAge` of one day.*


Firecrawl stores scraped pages and, by default,[returns a copy up to two days old](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/fast-scraping) instead of scraping again. When the same page has to go back into a prompt, for example when several workers build the same cached document block or a restarted process rebuilds it, a non-zero` maxAge` gives every caller the same bytes and so the same prefix hash. Keep` maxAge: 0` for content that has to be live, like prices.


Put the page content in the prompt and leave out the rest of the API response. Each Firecrawl response carries a unique` scrapeId` in its metadata, so a prompt built from the raw JSON changes on every call even when the page has not.


Keep each result small. Cache reads are cheap, but every new token is written once at 1.25x or 2x and then read on every later turn. In an[August 2026 analysis](https://primeline.cc/blog/claude-md-cache-cost) of 63,880 billed Claude Code requests, cache writes carried 76% of the cache-input cost inside a typical session, even with an aggregate hit rate of 96.59%. In our[Claude Code web research test](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/claude-code-web-research-tokens) , a stock-price lookup through Firecrawl's question format came back as 6 characters, against 295 characters from Claude Code's fetch tool for the same fact.


For document Q&A, load a whole documentation site into the prefix once, cache it, and ask many questions against it:


```text
import   anthropic
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


firecrawl   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  "fc-YOUR-API-KEY"  )
claude   =   anthropic  .  Anthropic  ()


# Crawl the docs once and join the pages as clean markdown
crawl   =   firecrawl  .  crawl  (
"https://docs.example.com"  ,
limit  =  50  ,
scrape_options  =  {  "formats"  : [  "markdown"  ],   "only_main_content"  :   True  ,   "max_age"  :   86_400_000  },
)
docs   =   "\n\n"  .  join  (page.markdown   for   page   in   crawl.data   if   page.markdown)


def   ask  (  question  :   str  )   ->   str  :
response   =   claude  .  messages  .  create  (
model  =  "claude-sonnet-5-5"  ,
max_tokens  =  1024  ,
system  =  [
{  "type"  :   "text"  ,   "text"  :   "Answer only from the documentation below."  },
{
"type"  :   "text"  ,
"text"  :   f  "<docs>  \n  {  docs  }  \n  </docs>"  ,
"cache_control"  : {  "type"  :   "ephemeral"  ,   "ttl"  :   "1h"  },
},
],
messages  =  [{  "role"  :   "user"  ,   "content"  : question}],
)
return   response  .  content  [  0  ].  text


print  (  ask  (  "How do I rotate an API key?"  ))
print  (  ask  (  "What are the rate limits on the free plan?"  ))    # reads the docs from cache
```


The crawl output stays fixed for the life of the cache because you build` docs` once and reuse the same string, and` max_age` (one day here) means a restart or a second worker rebuilds the same bytes. Clean markdown also keeps the cached block small. In our[tokenization benchmark](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/llm-tokenization-across-models) , fifteen pages came to 4.1 million tokens as raw HTML and 190,817 tokens as markdown. The 1-hour TTL fits a docs assistant where questions arrive minutes apart.


## How do you measure your cache hit rate?


Cache hit rate is cached input tokens divided by total input tokens, computed over a window of requests. Every provider returns the numbers on each response:


- **Anthropic:**` cache_read_input_tokens / (cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens)` . Anthropic's` input_tokens` counts only tokens after the last breakpoint, so all three belong in the denominator.
- **OpenAI:**` usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens / usage.input_tokens` , or the Prompt Caching Dashboard.
- **Gemini:**` usage.total_cached_tokens` against total input tokens.


Track the median per session as well as the aggregate. In the 63,880-request Claude Code analysis, the aggregate was 96.59% and the median session 86.41%, because a few very long sessions with near-perfect reuse pulled the total up.


When the rate drops, both major providers now tell you why:


- **Anthropic cache diagnostics** , generally available since[September 23, 2026](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/overview) : include a` diagnostics` object with the previous response's ID, and the API returns a` cache_miss_reason` saying whether the model, system prompt, tools, or message history diverged.[Fingerprints contain only hashes and token-count estimates](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/cache-diagnostics) .
- **OpenAI prompt cache diagnostics** : compares a request with a recent response and returns a reason such as` tools_changed` with the number of affected tokens.


Teams quoted in[OpenAI's GPT-6 caching announcement](https://openai.com/index/better-prompt-caching-for-gpt-6/) reported large changes from small fixes. Manus said its OpenAI cache hit rate went from about 85% to consistently above 90% in under a week. Wordsmith moved its session agents to explicit breakpoints and saw hit rates rise from 83% to 91%, cache writes fall by about two-thirds, and inference costs drop 36%. Strawberry Browser said a few percentage points of hit rate cut its costs 20%. GitHub said it had cut the share of Copilot prompt tokens needing fresh processing by more than 50%.


In a[July 2026 proxy study](https://systima.ai/blog/claude-code-vs-opencode-token-overhead) that reached[706 points on Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48883275) , OpenCode's request prefix was byte-identical in every captured run, while Claude Code rewrote tens of thousands of cache tokens mid-session and wrote up to 54x more cache tokens than OpenCode on the same task. Both harnesses set breakpoints correctly, so the gap came from how stable each kept its prefix.


## What 2026 research says about prompt caching


Provider caches require exact prefixes, and much of this year's research is about loosening that requirement for agents, whose prompts shift in ways a prefix cache can't reuse:


- **Cache-aware context management.**[TokenPilot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17016) (June 2026) points out that pruning and evicting context in agents changes the prompt layout and causes prefix mismatches, so token savings trade off against cache continuity. Its approach stabilizes the prefix and evicts in conservative batches, and reduced costs by 56-87% on PinchBench and Claw-Eval.
- **Caching tools independently of order.** Agents send tool and skill schemas in different combinations and orders, which defeats prefix caching.[ReCache](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19662) (August 2026) caches each schema separately with its own positions, matching dense performance (82.3% vs 82.4% invocation F1) with a 3.655x faster time to first token.
- **Position-independent caching.**[Irminsul](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05696) (May 2026) notes that agent workloads put identical tokens at shifted positions each turn, voiding prefix caches. Keying the cache by content instead of position recovered up to about 83% of prompt tokens beyond exact-prefix matching on agentic traffic.
- **Lifecycle-aware eviction.**[KVTether](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39819) (September 2026) tells the serving layer which messages an agent has discarded or will reuse soon, lowering estimated task cost by 33-40% against LMCache and MORI.
- **Reuse is not always free of side effects.**[Request Order Matters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05833) (October 2026) shows that non-prefix reuse with selective recomputation can make an unchanged prompt give different answers depending on earlier requests, with answer variation across orderings as high as 69%. The paper studies non-prefix reuse, which is a different technique from the exact prefix caching providers sell today.
- **Why the discount exists.**["Can I Buy Your KV Cache?"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13361) (June 2026) measured reuse at 9-50x cheaper in compute than prefill on Qwen3-4B, and argues the 0.1x cache-read price sits comfortably inside that range.


## When doesn't prompt caching help?


- **Short prompts.** Below 512 to 4,096 tokens, depending on provider and model, nothing caches.
- **One-shot requests with unique context.** If nothing is reused within the TTL, a write premium is a pure cost.
- **Sparse traffic.** Requests further apart than the cache lifetime miss every time, and on providers with a write premium they cost more than no caching.
- **Prompts that must change at the top.** Per-user system prompts can only share a cache within that user's requests. Move per-user content below the shared instructions so the shared part still caches across users.
- **Output-heavy workloads.** Caching only discounts input. If output dominates your bill, cap output and reasoning first.


Designing around the cache can also go too far, if it means keeping a worse context because it is cheap to resend. Cache the parts that are stable and correct, and clear stale tool results even when that costs a rebuild.[Context engineering vs prompt engineering](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/context-engineering) covers deciding what belongs in context in the first place.


## Prompt caching checklist


Check Why


Static content first: tools, instructions, documents, then history Prefix matching reuses only the unchanged start


No timestamps, IDs, or per-request values above the breakpoint One changed byte misses everything after it


JSON serialized with sorted keys Byte-different JSON is a different prefix


Tool list fixed per session; defer or restrict instead of removing Tools sit at the very start of the prefix


One model and one effort setting per session, or mid-conversation updates Caches are per model and per rendered settings


Side tasks forked from the parent prefix Otherwise compaction pays full price


TTL matched to measured gaps between requests Wrong TTL pays a write premium for nothing


Cache markers survive your gateway or proxy Stripped markers bill everything as uncached


Hit rate logged per request, alerted per day Drops cost money silently


Diagnostics turned on in staging Shows exactly where the prefix diverged
